blocks: Mog presents itself as a programming language for AI agents, with the public guide centered on embeddability, explicit capabilities, async host interaction, and native compilation.
Compared with mainstream application languages, Mog appears aimed less at general product development and more at constrained agent scripting and host-orchestrated workflows.

The official language guide frames Mog around a host-and-script model: the language stays relatively small while the host application provides capabilities such as I/O, HTTP, plugins, or ML operations.
This makes Mog notable less as "another general-purpose language" and more as a language design experiment for agent execution boundaries.
Capability-oriented design - Scripts declare what capabilities they require, and the guide describes those capabilities as the boundary for what code is allowed to do.
Ahead-of-time native compilation - The compiler documentation says Mog compiles to ARM64 and x86 binaries through rqbe, described there as a safe Rust implementation of the QBE backend.
Host-provided effects - The host provides capabilities and heavy operations, while the script focuses on coordination logic.
ML-adjacent data model - Mog includes tensor data structures, but the guide explicitly says the host provides the math and execution backend.
Mog programs describe behavior in the language and call into host capabilities for side effects or specialized operations.
Async capability calls are a first-class pattern in the public guide, which fits the agent and orchestration positioning.
Tensor values are built into the language as data containers, but advanced numerical work is expected to happen in the host environment.
Mog is just a tensor language -> False. Tensors are present, but the guide treats them as containers while the host performs the real computation.
Mog is a drop-in replacement for Python or JavaScript -> Not from the material I found. The official framing is much narrower and more host-driven.
Mog and Ash are direct comparables -> False. Mog is a language design for agent scripting; Ash Framework is an Elixir application framework.

A monorepo (monolithic repository) keeps many related packages, apps, or services in one version-control root instead of splitting each unit into its own repo.
Teams choose it to share CI, lint/format rules, internal libraries, and atomic cross-package changes—especially when releases must move several modules in lockstep.
Common in large product companies and open ecosystems (JS/TS with nx or GitHub/vercel/turborepo, Python workspaces, Rust workspaces, Go multi-module layouts).

Tension with multi-repo: monorepos reduce cross-repo coordination cost but raise demands on build graph performance, access control, and Dependency/Update/Automation / Software/Composition/Analysis at scale.
Workspace boundaries — Clear package names, ownership, and dependency rules so the graph stays navigable.
Task graph + caching — Incremental builds and remote cache (where available) keep CI and local dev tractable.
Policy for internal APIs — Shared libraries need semver or explicit consumer contracts so refactors do not silently break distant packages.
Workspace manifests — pnpm/yarn/npm workspaces, Poetry / uv workspace tables, Cargo workspaces, Bazel/Buck-style targets, etc., declare how packages resolve each other.
Orchestrators — Tools like nx and GitHub/vercel/turborepo schedule tasks, fan out tests, and dedupe work across the tree.
CI fan-out — Path filters, affected-only pipelines, and merge queues prevent “every push rebuilds the world” unless necessary.
One Git root shipping a mobile app, web app, and shared design-system package with a single design-token bump spanning all three.
PyPoetry/Concept/How to handle Monorepos in Poetry vs uv — language-specific packaging trade-offs inside a Python workspace.
“Monorepo = one deployable” — False; many deployables can live in one repo with separate release cadences.
“Monorepo fixes all coordination” — Oversold; you still need ownership, boundaries, and tooling discipline or the tree becomes a big ball of mud.
Statement: the number of transistors on an integrated circuit roughly doubles about every two years, with cost per transistor falling accordingly.
Origin: Gordon Moore (1965, revised 1975), co-founder of Intel; an observation and industry projection, not a law of nature.
Why it belongs here: often cited as if it were an axiom, but it is an observed regularity that has been slowing as physical limits approach—an illustration of how a named "law" can expire.
Logseq/Entity/Axiom — the contrast: statements that hold by proof or physical law.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

In today’s market, adopting new technology—particularly artificial intelligence—is often seen as a forward-thinking, strategic move. However, not every audience is equally receptive to this technological shift. Organizations embracing AI face hidden dangers, especially when their market’s moral compass differs sharply from their own expectations.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

This phenomenon, which we can describe as a “moral misread,” arises when companies underestimate the intensity or nature of the moral judgment their audience will apply to their actions. Unlike moral hazard, where insulated actors take excessive risks, and unlike moral panic, where society's reaction might be exaggerated, a moral misread occurs when the market's perception sharply diverges from a company's expectation, leading to unintended and often severe consequences.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads
Why AI Adoption is Particularly Vulnerable
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

Recent global data underscores that perceptions of AI vary significantly between regions. According to the 2025 AI Index, optimism about AI is notably high in Asia: 83% in China, 80% in Indonesia, and 77% in Thailand. Conversely, the U.S. trails significantly, with only 39% seeing AI as more beneficial than harmful. Such stark differences in sentiment indicate that adopting AI in less-optimistic markets like the U.S. can expose companies to heightened risks of moral misreads.

In January 2024, Duolingo laid off around 10% of its contract workforce as part of a strategic shift to become an "AI-first" company. The contractors, many of whom were involved in tasks like sentence writing and translation, were replaced by generative AI tools such as GPT-4. Duolingo’s leadership framed the move as an efficiency upgrade that would accelerate content development and improve scalability. However, public perception quickly turned critical.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads
The Case: Misjudging the Market Sentiment

Critics accused the company of prioritizing automation over human expertise and exploiting a trend at the expense of its workers. CEO Luis von Ahn later clarified that AI would not replace full-time roles and would instead serve to augment human productivity—but the reputational damage had already begun. The backlash stemmed not from the use of AI itself, but from the perceived disregard for the human labor that had helped build the platform. The incident even entered pop culture when comedian Josh Johnson joked about Duolingo’s layoff decision during a stand‑up set, highlighting how quickly corporate misreads can become fodder for public critique:

Duolingo isn’t alone. In 2017, Pepsi experienced a similar misread when it released an ad featuring Kendall Jenner. Intended as an expression of unity, the advertisement disastrously overlooked deep-seated public sentiment during the height of the Black Lives Matter protests. Instead of praise, the company was met with widespread condemnation.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

Other companies have also faced such backlash. Bud Light’s partnership with Dylan Mulvaney (ABC News) and Gillette’s "The Best Men Can Be" campaign (ABC Australia) faced polarizing reactions precisely because their strategies misunderstood or underestimated the moral lens of their audience.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

Companies adopting AI must carefully consider their audience's moral and cultural perceptions. Markets, especially those skeptical of AI, will judge not only technological proficiency but also the perceived moral implications of automation and AI-driven strategies.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

Recognizing the risk of moral misreads is crucial for any company looking to adopt AI. It’s essential to understand regional differences in perception, transparently communicate the motivations behind technological decisions, and thoughtfully address potential ethical concerns.
When the Market Judges: Navigating the Risks of AI Adoption and Moral Misreads

In a marketplace where moral judgments can shift rapidly, companies must tread carefully, informed not just by technological feasibility, but by a nuanced understanding of their audience’s moral outlook.

Jennie Livingston's documentary about New York City's 1980s ballroom scene and the Black and Latino queer people who built its houses, competitions, and performance styles.
The film was released in 1990 and selected for the U.S. National Film Registry in 2016 for preservation.

Its interviews and footage document ballroom participants' accounts of family, gender, race, class, and aspiration. The film's authorship and representation have also prompted debate about a white filmmaker documenting a community of color and about who receives recognition and economic benefit.
The film is an important source for understanding ballroom culture, but it is one documentary made from a particular perspective, not a complete account of the community.

A shared cache for cargo builds, run as the mbx command. Cargo still resolves dependencies, plans builds, and runs tools; mbx restores matching compiler outputs from one shared store and compiles the rest. No daemon or cache server is needed for local use.
Equivalent compilations share cache keys when checkout paths differ, so building one git worktree warms the next.
The store has a disk budget. Managed target/ directories are collected when their checkout disappears, goes unused, or exceeds its budget. mbx gc --dry-run previews a collection.
Independent Cargo commands share CPU and memory permits and deduplicate identical compilations in flight.

CI can reuse the cache through the GitHub/Action cache, a compatible cache server, or an S3-compatible bucket. jdx/mr-boxington-action sets it up. Pull request builds only read from a cache server or bucket; writes come from pushes to protected branches.
Install with mise (mise use --global --tool-option mr_boxington=true rust mr-boxington), or with cargo install mbx --locked followed by mbx setup.
Builds on ideas from sccache and kache; kache directly inspired its design.
Set the mr_boxington option on the rust tool and add mr-boxington as its own tool. Cargo then runs through mbx under mise exec, mise tasks, activated shells and mise's shims, with no mbx setup step.
Calling a toolchain's cargo directly, such as ~/.cargo/bin/cargo, skips mbx. Check with command -v cargo.
My global mise config turns it on: dotfiles#181.

Acousmatic music is a genre of electroacoustic music that is composed for playback via speakers, rather than being performed live by musicians with visible instruments. The listener engages with the pure sonic experience, unmediated by the visual cues of instrumental performance.
I use this term to refer to when I have a true musical experience. It applies to both making and listening to music.
Describes a scale with no semitones between adjacent steps. From the Greek an- ("without") and hēmitonion ("half tone").
The opposite is hemitonic: a scale with one or more semitone steps.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Anhemitonic: Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major and its modes, including Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Hemitonic: Music/Scale/Hirajoshi and the other Japanese in-scale pentatonics.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Music/Scale/Whole Tone is also anhemitonic. Every seven-note scale in twelve-tone equal temperament is hemitonic.

Bariolage is a string playing technique, primarily used on the Violin (but also on other bowed string instruments), characterized by rapid alternation between notes on adjacent strings—often between a static open string and varying stopped notes on a neighboring string.
Creates a shimmering or pulsating texture.
Common in Baroque and Classical music, notably in J.S. Bach’s solo string works.
Exploits the contrast in tone between open and fingered strings.
Often used to simulate polyphony or to add rhythmic drive.
In Bach’s Partita No. 3 in E major, BWV 1006, the Preludio uses bariolage extensively, alternating between the open E string and notes played on the A string.
From French barioler, meaning "to streak with several colors"—a metaphor for the tonal contrasts produced.

Scientific pitch notation names a pitch with a letter and an octave number: C4, G1, F♯5. The letter names the note, and the number says which octave of the whole audible range it sits in.
Middle C is C4, about 261.63 Hz. The A above it, A4, is the 440 Hz tuning note.
It is also called American standard pitch notation (ASPN) and international pitch notation (IPN).
The number goes up by one at each C. B3 is the note just below C4, and every note from C4 up through B4 carries the 4.
Each octave doubles the frequency: C3 is about 130.81 Hz, C4 about 261.63 Hz, C5 about 523.25 Hz.
An 88-key piano runs from A0 (27.5 Hz) to C8 (about 4186 Hz).
So a "low G" can be any of several notes. G1 (49 Hz) is a deep bass note near the bottom of a bass guitar's range; G3 (196 Hz) sits just below middle C.
MIDI sends a note as a number from 0 to 127 and leaves naming to the software. In scientific pitch notation, note 60 is C4, note 69 is A4, note 0 is C−1 and note 127 is G9.
Note number = 12 × (octave + 1) + semitones above C. G1 is 12 × 2 + 7 = 31, and F1 is 12 × 2 + 5 = 29.
The frequency of note m at A440 tuning is 440 × 2^((m − 69) / 12) Hz.
A note number carries no sharp or flat spelling. MIDI note 34 is both A♯1 and B♭1; the musical key decides which name to write.
